case.case_title: Dissanayake v. University of Sri Jayawardenapura and Two Others
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports [1986] 2 Sri L.R. 254

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the Vice-Chancellor’s order declaring the University premises out of bounds to the petitioner infringed the petitioner’s fundamental right to freedom of association under Article 14(1)(c).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that the restriction on his entry to the University premises violated his right to freedom of association as a student and student leader.
case_context.respondent_argument: The Vice-Chancellor argued that the restriction was a necessary disciplinary measure to maintain order and prevent disruption of examinations, and did not violate fundamental rights.
key_facts: Petitioner was declared out of bounds to University premises by the Vice-Chancellor.
The restriction followed charges of unauthorized publication and disruption of examinations.
Petitioner was a student leader representing student views.
The Vice-Chancellor relied on disciplinary powers under the Universities Act to maintain order.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court recognized that students do not lose their fundamental rights upon entering the University but that these rights are subject to reasonable regulation in light of the special characteristics of the University environment. The Vice-Chancellor’s disciplinary authority includes maintaining discipline and order, which may justify restrictions on association within University premises.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the restriction on the petitioner’s access to University premises was a lawful disciplinary action in response to his disruptive conduct. The restriction did not amount to an unlawful infringement of freedom of association as it was reasonably required to maintain discipline and order.
principles_established: Freedom of association is subject to reasonable regulation in the University context.
Disciplinary authority of the Vice-Chancellor includes power to restrict access to premises to maintain order.
Students’ fundamental rights must be balanced against the need for discipline and peaceful functioning of the University.

outcome.holding: The Court held that the Vice-Chancellor’s order restricting the petitioner’s access to University premises did not violate the petitioner’s freedom of association under Article 14(1)(c).

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 14(1)(c) was directly engaged because the petitioner’s claim involved his right to associate freely as a student within the University premises, which was restricted by the Vice-Chancellor’s disciplinary order.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court held that the Vice-Chancellor’s disciplinary powers to maintain order justified restricting the petitioner’s access to University premises, and this did not unlawfully infringe freedom of association.
